summary: For ages 9-10: read and write Roman numerals to 1000 (adding D=500, M=1000 and the subtractive pairs CD=400, CM=900), and read/write years such as MCMXCIX=1999 and MMXXIV=2024. The core skill is parsing chained additive and subtractive groups (M | CM | XC | IX) and understanding why, in the allowed pairs, a smaller symbol before a larger one means subtract. Keep a running contrast with base-ten place value: a year written in Roman is usually longer (though not always, e.g. MM for 2000) and is always awkward to calculate with compared with the compact four-digit numeral.
misconceptions: Invalid subtractive forms at scale (IC/IM for 99/999 instead of XCIX/CMXCIX).
Reading chained subtractive groups additively (misreading MCMXCIX).
Confusing D and M values or omitting a group.
Pure-additive over-long strings (writing 900 as DCCCC not CM).
Thinking Roman numerals gained a zero/place value.

activities.title: Build and decode years with a symbol-tile decoder
steps: Assemble a year from symbol tiles including D and M, or read a given year such as MCMXCIX.
Split the year into coloured groups (M | CM | XC | IX) and state each group's value (1000 + 900 + 90 + 9 = 1999).
Convert both directions: read a Roman year into Hindu-Arabic, and write a modern year (e.g. 2024 → MMXXIV) in Roman.
Try an illegal shortcut such as IC for 99, see it flagged, and correct it to XCIX.
activities.insight: A long, intimidating Roman year is really a chain of familiar subtractive/additive groups; each group reads independently, and only certain subtractive pairs are valid.

activities.title: Roman vs base-ten contrast panel
steps: Type or write a modern year and place its Roman form beside the compact Hindu-Arabic numeral.
Compare the length and readability of the two, and note that Roman lacks a zero and place value.
Try to imagine adding or multiplying two years in Roman form to feel why it is awkward.
activities.insight: A place-value system with zero is far more compact and calculation-friendly than additive/subtractive Roman notation.

activities.title: Read dates off real artefacts (guided)
steps: Look at dated monuments, film credits, foundation stones, or date inscriptions on clock towers that use Roman numerals (a clock face itself shows hours 1–12 rather than a year, and often writes 4 as IIII).
Decode each date into a modern year, saying how you split it into groups.
A guide or partner can read a date aloud and ask you to convert it, or ask you to write today's date in Roman.
activities.insight: Roman year notation appears in the real world; the same grouping skill decodes authentic dates.

checkQuestion: Ask: 'Why is four written IV and not IIII? Now read MCMXCIX for me — and tell me how you split it up to work it out.'
checkAnswer: IV = 4 because a smaller symbol placed before a larger one is subtracted (5 − 1). MCMXCIX = M(1000) + CM(900) + XC(90) + IX(9) = 1999, read as subtractive pairs.
